edits.name: Claude
edits.old: My primary tool and the one I would keep if I could keep one. But the more important point is this: most people are using Claude at surface level, basic prompts, generic outputs, no context. That is not what this tool is. The breadth is real but the depth is where it gets interesting, and building that depth takes deliberate effort. I have spent time learning how Projects and Skills work, how to write system prompts, how to set up an architecture that carries context across sessions. Claude Code is a different tool entirely: it reads your actual codebase and executes changes, the right escalation path when a Lovable prompt is not enough. Cowork sits across my drives so Claude has context on active projects without me re-explaining everything. Claude Design handles on-brand visual generation. Each of these required learning how it actually works rather than how the marketing describes it. That is the argument for going deep on one tool rather than skimming ten. Pick the tool that has the most surface area, understand its full architecture, and build your workflow around it. Claude has more surface area than anything else in this stack.

edits.name: Google Workspace AI
edits.old: Most useful in Sheets, where the AI features handle cell-by-cell editing jobs that would otherwise take forever, standardising data formats, cleaning inconsistent entries, reformatting columns. The Gemini side panel in Docs is genuinely useful for pulling in live data from Gmail or a connected spreadsheet without leaving the document. I use it to organise Drive for personal projects, which pairs well with Claude Cowork running across the same Drive. It is not the most powerful AI in the stack but it removes friction inside tools I am already living in.
